newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Br Biotech says drug aids survival.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Br Biotech says drug aids survival.

text.p: British Biotech Plc said on Monday there was "significant" evidence that its drug Marimastat boosted the chances of survival in cancer patients.

Finance director James Noble said in a telephone interview with Reuters that the company had been deliberately cautious in its statement, published earlier on Monday, interpreting the outcome of five clinical studies presented to a cancer conference in Vienna.

"We are extremely concerned not to raise patients' hopes of the drug," Noble said, but added that studies of Marimastat's impact on gastric, colo-rectal, ovarian and pancreatic cancer were "very encouraging, and the survival over 381 patients is very interesting."
"All of these were observations and have to be proved, but in many ways I think it is the most impressive data since the company was founded," Noble said.

The cautious nature of British Biotech's statement to the stock market disappointed some analysts, who said the data was just a confirmation of positive Phase II trial results published in May. The company's share price, which rocketed in May, slipped 14 1/2 pence to 217 in early afternoon trading.

But Noble said the scientific presentations made by doctors in Vienna contained much more detail. The studies covered 381 cancer patients who continued to take Marimastat, part of a new class of drug known as MMP inhibitors, after the 28-day period necessary to complete Phase II trials.

"There is no doubt that the people in our studies who took 10 miligrams twice a day (British Biotech's preferred dose) lived longer than those who took it once a day," Noble said, adding that "those patients who continued to take it for more than 28 days lived ... significantly longer" than those who stopped taking it.

Noble said the company was encouraged by Marimastat's apparent effectiveness across a range of cancers. "We are getting the same results for every cancer. There are five cancers and they all show roughly the same thing," he said.
He also played down concerns about the drug's side effects.
Some analysts were disappointed not to see more information on this aspect of the drug's action, which they said would be crucial to determining how acceptable Marimastat was to patients.

British Biotech confirmed that Marimastat caused joint pain, mainly in the arm and shoulder. The studies published in Vienna found that around 30 percent of patients taking 10 milligrams twice a day suffered side-effects after three to five months.

Noble said the pain varied from patient to patient, but added it "is not a serious problem. It is reversible." He said patients who suffered badly would be able to interrupt their treatment from time to time without any adverse impact.
Balancing the expectations of the stock market with the hopes of cancer sufferers resulted in Monday's statement being "a very difficult compromise between investors and patients," Noble said.

Although investors will have to wait until 1998 at the earliest for the result of Phase III, or late stage, trials into Marimastat, Noble said there would be a strong news flow to keep people informed in the interim. He said 13 separate Phase II studies are either underway or have been completed, with another six "starting in the next year."
British Biotech also planned to make presentations similar to those seen in Vienna every six months or so, he added.
